title: Three Terms, One Condition
statement: Among all complex numbers $z$ with $|z|=3$, find the largest possible value of $\left|z^{2}+8z-9\right|$.
hints: The condition $|z|=3$ and the constant term $-9$ in the expression are linked. Look for another way to write the number $9$ using $z$.
Use the conjugate identity $z\bar z=|z|^2$. Here it gives $9=z\bar z$, and after this substitution every term of $z^2+8z-9$ has a factor of $z$.

Substituting $9=z\bar z$ gives $z^2+8z-9=z(8+z-\bar z)$. Write $z=x+yi$ with $x,y$ real, so that $z-\bar z=2iy$. Then the modulus is $3\sqrt{64+4y^2}$, and it remains to find how large $y^2$ can be when $|z|=3$.
solution: Write $z=x+yi$ with $x,y$ real, so that $x^2+y^2=9$. For any complex number, $z\bar z=x^2+y^2=|z|^2$, so here $9=z\bar z$. Substituting this for the constant term gives $$z^2+8z-9=z^2+8z-z\bar z=z\left(8+z-\bar z\right).$$ Since $z-\bar z=(x+yi)-(x-yi)=2iy$, the second factor is $8+2iy$, which has real part $8$ and imaginary part $2y$. The modulus of a product is the product of the moduli, so $$\left|z^2+8z-9\right|=|z|\cdot|8+2iy|=3\sqrt{64+4y^2}.$$ This depends only on $y^2$ and increases as $y^2$ increases. Since $y^2=9-x^2\le 9$, we get $$\left|z^2+8z-9\right|\le 3\sqrt{64+36}=30.$$ Equality holds when $y^2=9$, that is, when $x=0$. For example, $z=3i$ satisfies $|z|=3$, and $z^2+8z-9=-9+24i-9=-18+24i$, which has modulus $\sqrt{18^2+24^2}=30$. The largest possible value is therefore $30$. Why this works. conjugate-modulus-identity, bounding: writing $9$ as $z\bar z$ lets $z$ factor out with fixed modulus, leaving a quantity that depends only on $y^2$, which is bounded by $9$.
